family: Aftermarket 1-DIN with a large dot-matrix display
examples: Sony CDX-GT with the FL dot matrix
one_liner: The best donor there is, and the cheapest way to a deck that does not look home-made.

price.v: £8–20 spares-or-repair; £30–60 working, which you do not need
price.why: Search “spares or repair”, “no CD”, “display dead”, “untested”. You are buying the box and the face.

window_w_mm.why: Varies by model. Measure with calipers.

chassis.why: Gives you the box, and usually the cage and trim ring too.

cage_included.v: often — pay a little more for one that has it
cage_included.why: A new cage is £8–15, so a £15 unit with one beats a £8 without.

buttons.v: typically 8–14 on a flexi matrix, plus a rotary knob
buttons.why: More than enough for the six-button ladder, with spares.

knob.v: rotary volume, usually an encoder or a pot with a detent feel
knob.why: Reuse the KNOB and fit your own EC11 behind it — the original's electrical type does not matter, only its shaft and cap do.

loading.v: ⚠️ usually BEHIND a fold-down front panel, not through a slot in it
loading.why: The late-1990s and 2000s flagships hide the disc behind the face: press a button, the panel drops, the slot is behind it. Confirmed in the general case for the Pioneer DEH-P9000R generation; confirm yours from the listing photographs.

hole_left.v: ✅ often NONE on the face itself — which is why this family has the best fascias
hole_left.why: If the disc loads behind the panel, the front is solid apart from its display window and its buttons. Nothing to fill.

best_use.v: pin the panel shut and use the window it already has
best_use.why: The window is 84–90 mm wide on these, which is what the deck wants. ⚠️ If the panel is MOTORISED, take the motor and gearbox out — it is depth you need and a mechanism you are not using. Then fix the panel closed rather than leaving it sprung.

keep_the_mechanism.why: See REUSE.md. The mechanism is dumb hardware that needs its servo, its DSP and its microcontroller, and those are the boards you are removing.

buttons.v: 8–14 on a carbon-pad flexi, plus the knob
buttons.why: More than the six the ladder needs, so you can pick the ones that feel best and blank the rest. ⚠️ Carbon-on-flexi is the fiddly kind — fine pitch, and it melts. Practise on a spare corner.

display_tech.v: LCD or VFD depending on model
display_tech.why: ⚠️ If it is a VFD, its power board makes tens of volts and holds them after power-off. See the hazards.

why: The window is already a wide letterbox of roughly the right size, in roughly the right place, and usually already amber on black — which is exactly what the deck draws.
They were made in enormous numbers and are worthless to everybody else once the CD mechanism jams, which is what makes them cheap.
The fascia has enough buttons to fill the ladder without drilling.

⚠️ One caution that applies to the whole family: several of these have a native display of 128×32, which is HALF the deck's 256×64 across. The physical window is usually close to right because our panel has a finer pitch — but 'usually close' is not 'measured', and this is the family where a few millimetres decides it.
watch_out: Motorised or flip-out fascias. The mechanism eats depth, it is fragile, and it is one more thing to defeat. Buy a fixed face.
Models where the CD slot dominates the front — the window is small and high, and the deck's panel wants the middle.
⚠️ VFD models: the inverter board. Discharge it and bin it.
steps: Take the fascia off FIRST, before any screws. Clips, not fasteners, and thirty years old. It is the part you cannot replace.
Unscrew the top and bottom covers and keep every screw — they are the right length for this chassis and nothing in your box will be.
Lift the whole internal assembly out before cutting anything, so you can see what holds what.
Bin the CD mechanism, the amplifier board and the main PCB. Discharge the large electrolytics first.
Keep the flexi from the button panel attached to the fascia and cut it free of the main board — you want the switches, not the matrix.
Lift the switch commons and wire each switch to its ladder resistor. Six buttons, six resistors, one wire to the deck.
Dry-fit the deck's panel behind the window before bonding anything, and check the lit area is centred in the aperture rather than in the fascia.

models.note: ⚠️ The display transformer is the hazard here, not the laser. Discharge it and bin it with the panel. The first car-audio OEL display Pioneer ever shipped, and the start of the whole look this project is chasing. Sought after, so not the cheapest — but the fascia is exactly right.

models.name: Pioneer MEH-P9000R
models.note: The 256 × 52 pixel count is the giveaway: at the usual 0.3 mm pitch that is a 76.8 × 15.6 mm lit area — the SAME WIDTH as the deck's 256 × 64 panel and 3.6 mm shorter. So its window is already the right width and wants opening by about 4 mm. This is the best-documented donor in the project. Cassette rather than CD, so the face has a tape door instead of a slot. The MiniDisc sibling of the DEH-P9000R with the same face. MiniDisc is worthless to everybody, which makes this the cheap way to that fascia.

reuse.value: £12–20 and a part you would otherwise buy
reuse.note: ⚠️ THE BIG ONE. Every CD-era head unit contains a 4-channel amplifier — usually a TDA7388, TDA7850 or similar — already bolted to the chassis as its heatsink and already wired to the ISO speaker connector. That is exactly the part BUILD.md tells you to go and buy. Cut the amp IC's four inputs free of the dead preamp and inject the deck's line out there instead. The IC datasheet gives the pinout; the mute/standby pin usually needs tying to its enable level, and that is the step people miss.

reuse.part: the rear ISO connectors and aerial socket
reuse.value: £8–15 of adapters, and a tidier back panel
reuse.note: The donor's own ISO 10487 A and B blocks and its DIN aerial socket are already mounted in the back panel and already the standard shape. Keeping them means the deck plugs into the car's loom with no adapter and no flying leads out of a hole.

reuse.value: hard to buy in the right shape
reuse.note: On most units the amplifier's heatsink IS part of the chassis casting. If you reuse the amp you get it for nothing; if you fit your own amp board, bolting it to the same casting is free cooling.

reuse.value: a pound, and some peace of mind
reuse.note: The reverse-polarity diode, the input fuse holder and the filter capacitors on the donor's power input are already rated for a car's supply. Cheap to buy, but they are already there and already fused.

⚠️ Usually NO, and it is worth understanding why before you try. Most head-unit displays are SEGMENT or character devices — fixed shapes and a few 5×7 cells — and they physically cannot show a 256×64 graphic screen. A genuine graphic dot-matrix panel can, but its controller is usually undocumented and its resolution is often 128×32, which is half the deck's width and would need a new layout tier in core/. ✅ The exception that IS supported: if the donor's panel turns out to be a Futaba GP1294AI, the firmware already has a driver — those are commonly sold as pulls from car radios.
If the donor had a remote, its TSOP-style receiver is already mounted behind the fascia with a clear line of sight. See HARDWARE.md §5c for the pin cost.
